Every experiment has the same basic shape — a set of coding tasks graded three ways (correctness 0/1/2, hallucination 0/1/2, compilable 0/1) — with one variable changed at a time: context size (EXP1), retrieval quality (EXP2), distractor type (EXP3), or compression approach (EXP4). # ERA: Embed, Route, Adapt for Cold-Start Cross-Model Latent Retrieval
Computer Science > Information Retrieval
[Submitted on 20 Nov 2026]
**Authors:** Venkata Chivukula, Zifeng Wang, Jinsung Yoon
## Abstract
Production retrieval systems are tied to the embedding model that indexed their corpus. Moving queries to a different encoder normally requires re-embedding the whole corpus, and at cold start there are no query logs while every document embedded by the new encoder incurs an API or compute cost. We present ERA (Embed, Route, Adapt), a system for cold-start cross-model latent retrieval. ERA spends a small anchor budget on maximally informative documents, selected from the existing target index via Cosine Farthest Point Sampling, trains a lightweight adapter with a Manifold Alignment Loss that couples directional alignment with orthogonal regularization to prevent representation collapse, and pairs the adapter with a deterministic router that escalates the rare, hard queries that define perceived retrieval quality. Across five BEIR datasets, ERA matches or outperforms point-wise L2 and embedding-conversion baselines, with relative gains of up to 35% nDCG@10 on Arguana, and on clustered corpora its anchor selection also improves prior methods under a fixed anchor budget. With 1.2 ms of adapter and router overhead on top of a ~20 ms local encoder, ERA at a 20% nominal escalation budget reduces end-to-end query latency from roughly 160 ms to 38-86 ms while concentrating escalations on the queries where the projection fails most.

We conduct extensive experiments with five embedding models from three model families on the MAIR benchmark (Sun et al. 2024), spanning 126 retrieval tasks across six domains, and show that ERA improves average nDCG@10 by up to 8% over zero-shot retrieval for symmetric embedding pairs in low-label settings while outperforming methods that require more labeled data.
*    •
We show that ERA, despite being a linear weight, effectively combines stronger query embedders with weaker document embedders, including across different model families, by bridging both the representation gap between embedding models and the semantic gap between complex queries and simple documents, improving average nDCG@10 by up to 12% over zero-shot retrieval of the document embedder without expensive corpus re-indexing.

To address the challenges of retrieval adaptation under query-document complexity asymmetry, we propose Efficient Retrieval Adapter (ERA), a novel framework for training retrieval adapters in a label-efficient manner. In this section, we first formulate the problem of retrieval with an adapter, and then describe the design principles of ERA, followed by our training recipe.

We propose Efficient Retrieval Adapter (ERA), a novel framework for training retrieval adapters in a label-efficient manner to address the challenges of retrieval adaptation under query-document complexity asymmetry. ERA employs a two-stage training process, self-supervised alignment training and supervised adaptation, to effectively bridge the representation gap between different embedding models and the semantic gap between complex queries and simple documents. Our experiments demonstrate that ERA efficiently and effectively improves retrieval performance across various models, domains, and label resource settings, and enables asymmetric retrieval with different query and document embedders without the need for re-indexing the corpus.

Dense retrieval systems increasingly face an asymmetry between complex instruction-like queries and relatively simple, static document collections. ## Abstract
Production retrieval systems are tied to the embedding model that indexed their corpus. Moving queries to a different encoder normally requires re-embedding the whole corpus, and at cold start there are no query logs while every document embedded by the new encoder incurs an API or compute cost. Backward-compatible retrieval enables a new encoder to query the gallery that an old model has already encoded, so that a cross-modal retrieval system can be upgraded without re-encoding billions of items. Existing compatible methods either fit the old query and stay near the accuracy of the old model, or run the old and the new encoder for every query.
